what: FUNDING.md 6.8: each lender's cushion over the ten crash windows. Money in USD. Health factors and shares in basis points (10000 is a health factor of 1.0). A minute counts the window's one-minute closes from 0. `table` is the README's: for each lender and cushion, the worst of the ten windows with no top-up and with top-ups that land 2, 15 and 60 minutes after they are ordered.

lenders.name: Rhea
lenders.source: Liquidation line 76%: nBTC's volatility ratio 8000 times USDC's 9500, in Rhea's health factor sum(c*p*vol)/sum(b*p/vol) (research/rhea.md items 3 and 4 and section 11, read on mainnet 10 Nov 2026; FUNDING.md 6.3). Discount 0.3%: the figure research/scripts/rhea_warehouse.py uses in the last block of report(). Rhea's own rule is (1 - HF)/2, with no close factor, and the slices seen on chain were $150-250 at 0.24-0.28% (research/rhea.md items 3 and 9).

lenders.name: Aave (Ethereum)
lenders.source: WBTC on Aave v3 Ethereum (core): liquidation threshold 0.85 and liquidation bonus 0.05, from Aave's own API as saved in research/data/aave_live_2026-11-10.json (research/aave.md, 'Bitcoin as collateral'). Close factor: up to 50% of the whole debt, or all of it once the health factor is 0.95 or lower; the collateral taken is the debt covered times the bonus (research/aave.md, 'Facts for the build').

assumptions: The book: the worked example (FUNDING.md 2). $100,000 of bitcoin posted at the lender and a $100,000 BTC short on Hyperliquid, both at the window's starting price, before its first one-minute close (as `backtest crash` draws its loans). The lender's loan is the most that keeps the health factor at the cushion being tested (risk_core::lender::limit_micro, rounded down), so the first minute's price already moves it. Our own pool's part of the loan, Hyperliquid's margin and the short's own liquidation are not modelled here: `backtest crash` covers them.

Prices: BTC's path in the engine's own replay of each window (RISK_ENGINE.md 4.5): the recorded one-minute closes, 240 a window, kept as parts per billion of the starting price. Both lenders are taken to price the bitcoin as BTC: Rhea reads Pyth's BTC/USD for nBTC (research/rhea.md 11); for Aave's WBTC it is our reading. So the replay's 2% bridge depeg and its perp gap are not applied. A lender sees each minute's close and nothing inside the minute; its price feed is never late or wrong.

Health factor: the collateral's value times the lender's liquidation ratio, over the debt, in basis points rounded down (risk_core::lender::hf_bp). The lender liquidates under 10000. No interest accrues over the four hours (at Rhea's 15.91% it is under $4 on $50,667), and gas is left out.

Order within a minute: the price moves; the lender liquidates at the new price if the health factor is under 1.0; then a top-up due that minute lands; then our check runs and may order the next top-up. So a top-up that lands in the minute the lender liquidates comes second, and counts as late.

Top-ups: our check runs once a minute. When the health factor is under 1.35 (risk_core::lender::ACT_HF_BP) and no top-up is on its way, one is ordered: a repayment sized to bring the health factor back to 1.5 (TARGET_HF_BP) at that minute's price (repay_to_target_micro). It lands 2, 15 or 60 minutes later with the amount ordered, whatever the price did meanwhile, never more than is still owed; the next can be ordered at that same minute's check. A cushion that starts under 1.35 orders its top-up at minute 0. The 1.2 level (NOW_HF_BP) changes nothing here: it is the same plan with the same delay. A top-up due after the window's last minute does not land.

The top-up's money is taken to be there. The backtest does not check that Hyperliquid has it to send: in a fall the short's winnings are about twice what a top-up from 1.35 to 1.5 needs, but a top-up ordered at minute 0 (cushions 1.2 and 1.3) has no winnings behind it and must come from the client's own USDC.

Rhea's liquidators: in every minute the health factor is under 1.0 they repay just enough debt to bring it back to 1.0 at that minute's price, and take collateral worth the repayment / (1 - 0.3%): the formula of research/scripts/rhea_warehouse.py, taken = (debt - 0.76 x collateral) / (1 - 0.003 - 0.76). A minute's slices are added into one. Rhea's own rule is a discount of (1 - HF)/2 and a health factor left just under 1.0 (research/rhea.md 3); the flat 0.3% understates the cost in a minute that gaps far under 1.0 (each case's `lowest_liquidation_hf_bp` shows how far it went).

Aave's liquidator: in a minute the health factor is under 1.0, one liquidator repays the most allowed, half the debt, or all of it when the health factor is 0.95 or lower, and takes collateral worth that plus the 5% bonus (WBTC on Ethereum). Taking the most allowed is our reading: a liquidator is paid by size. If the collateral cannot cover it, all of it is taken and debt is left. Which Aave version runs on Ethereum is not confirmed (research/aave.md), and newer versions' special rules for small positions are not modelled.

The hedge: the liquidators keep the bitcoin they take and nobody trims the short during the window. `collateral_sold` is the bitcoin taken, each slice at the price of its minute. `penalty` is that less the debt it repaid. `short_uncovered` is the bitcoin sold at the window's last price: the part of the short with no bitcoin behind it then. `btc_sold_bp` is the share of the bitcoin, which is also the share of the short.

The second table does not depend on where a window happens to start. `worst_falls` is BTC's worst fall over the closes a top-up is exposed to, from the start or any minute of any window: its delay plus one, because the position was last seen at or over the act level one close before the check that orders the top-up, and the lender sees every close up to the minute it lands, before it lands. A top-up ordered from a health factor under `level_needed_bp` could come too late. `levels_hold` is the longest whole-minute delay each of the engine's levels survives that way. Both are the same for every lender: a fall moves every health factor by the same share. Falls that run past a window's 240 minutes are not seen.

The table's worst case, for each lender, cushion and mode, is the window where the lender sold the most collateral (the first of equals). Its lowest health factor column is the position left alone by everyone, the lender too.
notes: Each mode's cell is the worst of the ten windows: the collateral the lender's liquidators sold (and its share of the bitcoin), what the discount or bonus cost, and the short left uncovered (the bitcoin sold, at the window's last price); then how many windows liquidated. "none (lowest x)" is no liquidation, and the lowest health factor the lender saw.
A top-up is ordered when the health factor is under 1.35 and repays enough to bring it back to 1.5 at that minute's price. A cushion that starts under 1.35 (1.2 and 1.3 here) orders it at minute 0.
